new_statements.citation: Reed, Wes (data checked by; SIL PNG Branch). 2000. Organised Phonology Data: Yopno Language [YUT], Morobe Province. 4 pp. Manuscript, SIL Ukarumpa (PDF printed 21 Sep 2004). SIL Language & Culture Archives entry 42339.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (4 pp., native text, PDF metadata: Title "OPD", Author "SIL PNG Branch", created 2004-09-20). Page 3 (header "Yupna (Yopno) OPD Printed: September 21, 2004 Page 3") contains, verbatim, the heading "Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)" followed by the single line "Stress is contrastive occurring on first or second syllable." Nothing else on stress, tone or length in that section; the only other prosodic remark is under Conventions: Phonological, "/ɨ/ is inherently longer than other vowels." No stressed forms or minimal pairs anywhere in the OPD (the consonant/vowel example lists and the syllable-pattern list are unmarked for stress). The heading is the OPD template heading, so sile…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is lexically contrastive; it falls on either the first or the second syllable of the word, and which one is not predictable from the source's statement (no rule, no minimal pairs and no stressed examples are given). Note that Claassen & McElhanon 1970: 66 judged stress 'probably sub-phonemic in Yupna' with a light functional load, so the contrastiveness claim is not uncontested.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned; the one-line statement gives no examples. The OPD notes /ɨ/ is inherently longer than other vowels and says nothing about tone. Claassen & McElhanon 1970: 66 (survey) say 'Stress is phonemic in Rawa but probably sub-phonemic in Yupna and Wantoat. In none of these languages does it carry a heavy functional load.'
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (the OPD's phonemic-inventory format lists stress under word suprasegmentals); no phrase-level statement. Data is the SIL Keweng/Tepmangi-area variety (major villages listed: Keweng, Tepmangi, Nokopo, Gua, Isan, Wandabo); the OPD header calls the language 'Yupna (Yopno)'.
new_statements.identity_note: Reed 2000 OPD describes 'Yopno Language [YUT]', header 'Yupna (Yopno)', Morobe Province, villages Keweng, Tepmangi, Nokopo, Gua, Isan, Wandabo -- i.e. the SIL working variety of Yopno = yopn1238 (dialects Kewieng, Nokopo, Wandabong, Isan per Wikipedia). Claassen & McElhanon 1970 use 'Yupna' for the same language. Slotta's materials are on the Nian/Nokopo dialect.

tone_statements.quote: Domung does not exhibit lexical or grammatical tone, which is not surprising since no other Finisterre languages exhibit tone. ... As would therefore be expected, a review of 16 analyzed Finisterre family languages reveals that tone systems are absent as shown in Table 29. ... [Table 29, Yupna group:] Yopno [yut] (Reed 1993, 2000a) | Tonal: No | Lexical accent system: Accent is reported to be contrastive, but occurring on first or second syllable
tone_statements.locator: p. 67, section 7 'Tone and Accent' (first sentence) and 7.1 (p. 67, 'a review of 16 analyzed Finisterre family languages..'); p. 69, Table 29, Yupna group, row 'Yopno [yut] (Reed 1993, 2000a)'; stress remark p. 70, Table 30
tone_statements.summary: No tone; lexical (contrastive) accent on 1st or 2nd syllable (after Reed 1993, 2000a).

tone_statements.citation: Amha, Azeb, James Slotta & Hannah S. Sarvasy. 2021. Singing the Individual: Name Tunes in Oyda and Yopno. Frontiers in Psychology 12: 667599 (7 pp.). doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2021.667599
tone_statements.quote: The konggap are sung, whistled, and hummed throughout the day as people summon others, alert them to their presence, or even think about them. The Yopno language is non-tonal and konggap bear no phonic relation to people’s proper names. Rather, each is a melodic and rhythmic sequence that identifies its bearer uniquely in a way that proper names do not ... [p. 4:] These pitch contours are not directly reminiscent of the prosodic contours of any linguistic units in either language.
tone_statements.locator: p. 2 (end of section 'Yopno Name Tunes: konggap', sentence runs on to p. 3 after Table 1); second sentence p. 4, section 'Formal Qualities'
